question: What fasting plasma glucose level confirms diabetes?
answer: A fasting plasma glucose of ≥ 7.0 mmol/L is in the diabetes range [p. 32]. Fasting means no caloric intake for at least 8 hours [p. 32]. In people without symptoms, repeat the test to confirm the diagnosis, preferably with the same test, as soon as practicable on a subsequent day [p. 32].

question: What HbA1c range defines prediabetes?
answer: Prediabetes (intermediate hyperglycaemia) is defined by an HbA1c of 5.7–6.4% [p. 32]. Diabetes is defined as an HbA1c of ≥ 6.5% [p. 32].

question: At what age should testing for diabetes begin in adults without risk factors?
answer: Testing should begin at age 35 years for all other patients, meaning those without the listed risk factors [p. 31]. If results are normal, testing should be repeated at a minimum of 3-year intervals, with more frequent testing considered depending on initial results and risk status [p. 31].

question: How often should women who had gestational diabetes be tested for diabetes afterwards?
answer: Women who were diagnosed with GDM should have lifelong testing at least every 3 years [p. 31]. Note: the guideline never mentions: afterwards.

question: How much aerobic physical activity per week is recommended for adults with diabetes?
answer:
Most adults with type 1 and type 2 diabetes should do 150 minutes or more of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week. This should be spread over at least 3 days, with no more than 2 consecutive days without activity [p. 29][p. 43].

Younger and more physically fit individuals may manage with shorter durations of vigorous-intensity or interval training, with a minimum of 75 minutes per week [p. 29].

For people with type 2 diabetes, the guideline specifies 150 minutes of aerobic exercise per week at 50 to 70% of maximal heart rate, plus resistance training three times per week [p. 43].

question: What is the starting dose of basal insulin when initiating insulin in type 2 diabetes?
answer:
Start basal analog insulin or NPH insulin at bedtime [p. 48]. The starting dose is 10 international units/day or 0.1-0.2 IU/kg/day [p. 48]. Titrate to fasting blood glucose by increasing 2 units every 3 days until the fasting target is reached [p. 48]. If hypoglycemia occurs, determine the cause and reduce the insulin dose by 10-20% [p. 48].

question: What is the starting dose of premixed insulin in type 2 diabetes?
answer:
The excerpts give no fixed starting dose for premixed insulin. Where basal insulin is not an option, premixed insulin can be started with the largest meal [p. 49].

A figure covers changing from basal insulin to twice-daily premix before breakfast and supper. It says to divide the current basal dose into 2/3 in the morning and 1/3 in the evening, or possibly a different split, because the text is garbled [p. 48].

After starting, titrate at most twice a week. Adjust human insulin by no more than 4 U per week and analogue insulin by no more than 6 U per week [p. 49].

question: By how much can human premixed insulin be adjusted per week in adults?
answer: Adjust human premixed insulin by no more than 4 U per week in adults [p. 49]. Titrate at least once, but not more than twice, each week [p. 49]. Titrate slowly to avoid hypoglycaemia, using 2-4 Units per dose [p. 49].

question: What blood pressure goal should medical treatment maintain in people with diabetes?
answer: Medical treatment should maintain a blood pressure goal of <140/90 mm Hg [p. 66]. The goal may be lower (e.g., 130/80 mm Hg) in patients at high risk of cardiovascular disease (ASCVD or 10-year ASCVD score ≥15%) [p. 66]. In pregnancy, the goal is 110–135/85 [p. 66]. Therapeutic lifestyle changes should be reviewed if BP is >120/80 mm Hg [p. 66].

question: Which statin intensity is recommended for primary prevention in people with diabetes aged 40 to 75 years?
answer:
Moderate-intensity statin therapy is recommended, in addition to lifestyle therapy, for people with diabetes aged 40–75 years without ASCVD [p. 67].

High-intensity statin is reasonable for those at higher risk, meaning multiple ASCVD risk factors or age 50–70 years [p. 67].

If 10-year ASCVD risk is ≥20%, it may be reasonable to add ezetimibe to maximally tolerated statin therapy [p. 67].

Moderate-intensity examples include atorvastatin 10–20 mg and rosuvastatin 5–10 mg [p. 67].

question: What aspirin dose is recommended for secondary prevention when ASCVD is present?
answer: Aspirin 75 to 162 mg daily is recommended for secondary prevention if ASCVD is present [p. 67]. Clopidogrel 75 mg is the alternative if the patient is intolerant to aspirin [p. 67].

question: At what blood glucose level should people on insulin check for ketones?
answer: People with type 1 diabetes, and people with type 2 diabetes on multiple daily insulin injections, should check for ketones any time their blood glucose is >16 mmol/l, or if they are unwell [p. 61]. They should have blood ketone monitoring devices, or urine dipsticks if devices are not available [p. 61]. Check the figure on page 61 before acting.

question: On a sick day, how many extra units of insulin should a 70 kg patient with blood ketones of 3.0 or more take?
answer: For a patient whose total daily dose can't be determined, body weight is used to estimate the extra insulin needed [p. 61]. A 70 kg patient with blood ketones of 3.0 or more falls in the 20% column and should take 14 extra units [p. 61]. For comparison, blood ketones of 1-2.9 call for 7 units (10%) [p. 61]. question: When should retinopathy screening start in type 1 diabetes?
answer: Screening for retinopathy (a dilated eye exam) should start at puberty or from age 11 years, whichever is earlier, once the child has had diabetes for 2–5 years [p. 137]. For retinopathy, the guideline says to repeat it every 2–3 years [p. 137].

question: How should hypoglycaemia be treated in a patient who is conscious and able to swallow?
answer:
For a child who is conscious and able to swallow and take direction (from the school plan):

- If in doubt or unable to test, assume it is a hypo and treat immediately. [p. 209]
- Give easily absorbed carbohydrate, e.g., sugar, glucose, juice, sweet or soda. [p. 209]
- Do not use fat-containing foods such as chocolate, milk, ice-cream or biscuit, because absorption is slow. [p. 209]
- Retest blood glucose after 15 minutes. If it is still below 4 mmol/L, repeat the sweet treatment. [p. 209]
- Once it is above 4 mmol/L, give a snack or meal if due within 1 hour. Otherwise give longer-acting carbohydrate: 1 slice of bread, half a banana, 200 ml of milk or a medium apple. [p. 209]

question: What dose of glucagon is given for severe hypoglycaemia in a child weighing more than 25 kg?
answer:
For severe hypoglycemia, if glucagon is available, give it SC or IM. The dose is 1 mg for a child of 25 kg or more, and 0.5 mg for under 25 kg [p. 157].

The weight threshold was garbled in the OCR text, so the "25 kg or more" reading is an interpretation.

question: What fasting blood glucose range diagnoses gestational diabetes?
answer: A fasting blood glucose of 5.1-6.9 mmol/L (92-125 mg/dL) meets the criteria for gestational diabetes mellitus [p. 96]. A fasting value of ≥ 7 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) falls under diabetes in pregnancy instead [p. 96].

question: When should universal screening for gestational diabetes be done?
answer:
Universal screening should be done at 24-28 weeks of pregnancy, or at first contact if the woman presents late [p. 97]. The screening test is a 75-g OGTT, given after an 8-hour overnight fast, with blood glucose measured at 1 hour and 2 hours [p. 97].

A woman with more than one risk factor should have an RBS/FBS/OGTT at first contact [p. 97].

question: How is diabetic ketoacidosis defined in adults?
answer:
The guideline defines diabetic ketoacidosis as hyperglycemia over 13.9 mmol/l, a bicarbonate level below 18 mEq/L and a pH below 7.30, with ketonemia and ketonuria [p. 182].

If ketosis or ketoacidosis occurs with normal sugars, it advises considering euglycemic DKA [p. 182].

question: How much potassium should be added to the infusion in DKA when potassium is 3.5 to 5.5 mmol/L?
answer: Add 40 mmol of KCl per litre of fluid, up to a maximum of 0.5 mmol/kg/hr [p. 125]. Start after the initial volume expansion (after the first hour), at the same time as insulin [p. 125]. The potassium replacement table also gives 40 mmol per litre of infusion solution for a potassium of 3.5-5.5 mmol/L [p. 183]. Monitor potassium every 2-4 hours [p. 125].

question: What urine albumin creatinine ratio is severely increased albuminuria?
answer:
Severely increased albuminuria is an ACR above 30 mg/mmol [p. 69]. Moderately increased is from ≥2.5 mg/mmol in males or ≥3.5 mg/mmol in females up to 30 mg/mmol [p. 69]. Mildly increased is below those male and female cut-offs [p. 69].

question: Above what GFR should an SGLT2 inhibitor be started for persistent proteinuria?
answer: For persistent proteinuria or microalbuminuria, start an SGLT2 inhibitor if the GFR is above 20 ml/min [p. 69]. An ACE inhibitor is also started for this indication [p. 69].

question: How often should all people with diabetes be seen by a foot specialist?
answer: All patients with diabetes should be seen by a foot specialist at least once a year [p. 78].

question: What random blood glucose level diagnoses diabetes in a TB patient with classical symptoms?
answer:
In a TB patient with no known history of diabetes, a random blood sugar (RBS) of 11.1 mmol/L or more, together with classical symptoms of diabetes, indicates diabetes [p. 93]. The guideline says random glucose should only be used in patients with symptoms [p. 32].

If the RBS is 5.6 mmol/L or more but below 11.1 mmol/L, the TB clinic pathway goes on to a 75 g OGTT, with or without HbA1c [p. 93].

question: How long before Ramadan should a person with diabetes have a pre-Ramadan visit?
answer:
The guideline gives two slightly different timings on the same page. One passage says the pre-Ramadan visit should be at least 8 weeks before Ramadan [p. 101]. The assessment flowchart says all individuals seeking to fast should attend a pre-Ramadan visit 6-8 weeks before Ramadan [p. 101]. Both agree on a visit of about 8 weeks before, but they differ on whether 6 weeks is acceptable.

The visit is used to stratify risk and develop an individualised management plan [p. 101].
